subject: History of Pakistan & India
title: 1. Muslim Rule and Heritage in India (712–1857)

segments.text: This topic covers eleven and a half centuries — longer than any other topic in the syllabus — and it sets up almost everything that follows. The institutions the British eventually took over (a land-revenue system, a service nobility, a body of provincial administration), the demographic and cultural facts that later made partition conceivable (a large, geographically concentrated Muslim population with its own political memory), and the very idea that religious community could be a basis for political claims, all have roots in this period. A candidate who treats it only as a sequence of dynasties will struggle with every later topic; a candidate who understands it as the building and eventual weakening of a durable state system will find Topics 2 through 5 much easier to explain.

blocks.text: Background: The Subcontinent Before Sustained Muslim Rule

segments.text: Before 712 CE, the Indian subcontinent had no single political centre. Political power was fragmented among regional kingdoms — in the north, dynasties such as the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas of Bengal, and various Rajput principalities contested territory; in the Deccan and south, the Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Pallavas and later the Cholas built their own regional states. Society was organised through the caste system, temple-centred religious and economic life, and a strong tradition of regional kingship legitimated through Brahmanical ritual. This fragmentation matters for understanding what followed: there was no single “Indian empire” for Muslim rulers to displace. Instead, incoming Muslim power entered a patchwork of competing regional states, allied with some, defeated others, and was itself repeatedly absorbed into regional politics rather than imposed as a single uniform system from outside.

At the same time, in the Arabian Peninsula and the wider Middle East, the seventh century saw the rise of Islam under the Prophet Muhammad (570–632 CE) and the rapid expansion of Muslim political power under the Rashidun and then the Umayyad Caliphate. By the early eighth century, Umayyad power stretched from Spain to Central Asia. The conquest of Sindh has to be understood as one edge of this much larger imperial expansion — a frontier campaign of the Umayyad Caliphate, not an isolated event in Indian history alone.

blocks.text: From Sindh to the Sultanate: The Long Build-Up (711–1206)

segments.text: The Arab conquest of Sindh.

In 711–712 CE, a young Umayyad commander, Muhammad bin Qasim, led a campaign into Sindh on the orders of the governor of Iraq, Hajjaj bin Yusuf. The immediate trigger usually cited is a dispute over the treatment of Arab traders and pilgrims — accounts describe Arab ships being attacked near Debal (close to modern Karachi) and Hajjaj using this as grounds for military action against Raja Dahir, the ruler of Sindh. Muhammad bin Qasim defeated Dahir, captured key towns including Debal, Nerun, Aror and Multan, and established Umayyad rule over Sindh and southern Punjab.

What matters for the exam is not the campaign narrative alone but its significance: this was the first durable Muslim political foothold in South Asia, administered initially as a frontier province of the Umayyad, then Abbasid, Caliphate. It did
not

immediately extend Muslim rule over the rest of the subcontinent — Sindh remained a distant, semi-autonomous frontier for the next three centuries, eventually passing to local Arab and then non-Arab dynasties as Abbasid central control weakened. Treating 712 as the start of one continuous empire is the single most common error candidates make with this topic.
From raids to conquest: Ghaznavids and Ghurids.

The next major wave came from Central Asia rather than Arabia. Mahmud of Ghazni (ruled 998–1030) led a famous series of campaigns into north-western India, most remembered for the repeated raids into Punjab and the 1025 raid on the Somnath temple in Gujarat. Historians read Mahmud’s motives in more than one way: contemporary court chronicles emphasise religious merit and iconoclasm, while modern historians (for example Romila Thapar’s extended study of the Somnath episode) point out that temple treasuries were also major concentrations of wealth in this period, so plunder and legitimation through religious language often operated together rather than as alternatives. What is not disputed is the outcome: Mahmud annexed Punjab to the Ghaznavid empire but did not attempt to conquer the interior of India, so his raids should be understood as wealth-extraction and frontier expansion rather than the founding of settled Muslim rule over India as a whole.

Settled Muslim political rule over northern India began later, with the Ghurid dynasty. Muhammad Ghuri (also called Muizz ud-Din Muhammad) invaded India repeatedly from the 1170s, was defeated by the Rajput confederacy under Prithviraj Chauhan at the First Battle of Tarain (1191), but returned the following year and decisively defeated Prithviraj at the Second Battle of Tarain (1192). This second battle is the conventional turning point: Ghurid generals, especially the slave-commander Qutb-ud-din Aibak, then extended control over Delhi, Ajmer and much of the Gangetic plain. When Muhammad Ghuri was assassinated in 1206, Aibak, who had governed Ghurid territories in India as a trusted commander, established himself as an independent ruler in Delhi — conventionally treated as the founding moment of the Delhi Sultanate.

blocks.text: The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526): Building a State

segments.text: The Sultanate period is best learned as a sequence of five dynasties, each of which faced the same underlying problem in a different way: how does a relatively small ruling elite of Turkic, Afghan and (later) local converts govern a vast, religiously and culturally diverse subcontinental population, defend against external threats (chiefly the Mongols), and prevent its own military aristocracy from fragmenting the state?
The Mamluk (Slave) dynasty (1206–1290).

Qutb-ud-din Aibak began the dynasty; his most important successor, Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236), is usually credited with actually consolidating Delhi Sultanate rule — securing recognition from the Abbasid Caliph, developing the iqta system of assigning revenue-bearing land to nobles in exchange for military service, and defending Delhi from the first waves of Mongol pressure under Genghis Khan’s forces. Razia Sultana (r. 1236–1240), Iltutmish’s daughter, is a notable exception in a male-dominated succession pattern, though her short reign ended in a nobles’ revolt — a useful example of how the Turkish military aristocracy (the “Chihalgani” or Forty) constrained even a capable ruler’s authority. Ghiyas-ud-din Balban (r. 1266–1287) developed an elaborate theory of divine kingship (zill-i-ilahi, “shadow of God”) to strengthen royal authority against the nobility, alongside a harsh internal-security policy and continued Mongol defence.
The Khalji dynasty (1290–1320).

Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296–1316) is the dynasty’s dominant figure. His reign shows the Sultanate at its most centralising: he introduced market-control regulations (fixing prices of grain, cloth and horses to maintain a large standing army affordably), reorganised land revenue assessment, and built a large, disciplined army that decisively defeated repeated Mongol invasions — arguably the single most important achievement of any Sultanate ruler, since a Mongol conquest of Delhi would have altered the entire subsequent history of the region. He also extended Sultanate authority deep into the Deccan through campaigns led by his general Malik Kafur.
The Tughlaq dynasty (1320–1414).

Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325–1351) is remembered for two controversial policies often mishandled in students’ answers: the transfer of the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan (intended to better govern the empire’s southern territories, but executed in a way that caused severe hardship and was eventually reversed), and the introduction of token currency (copper or brass coins declared equal in value to silver, an idea with sound economic logic — similar to modern fiat currency — but undermined by weak controls against forgery, which forced its withdrawal). These episodes are best explained as ambitious but poorly implemented reforms rather than simple “mistakes of a mad king,” a dated and overly personalised framing. Firoz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351–1388) pursued a more consolidating, less experimental policy: he undertook major public works (canals, hospitals, rest-houses), reorganised taxation along lines more consistent with Islamic jurisprudence, and is credited with an extensive programme of city-building, though later Tughlaq rulers proved weak and the dynasty fragmented — Timur’s devastating sack of Delhi in 1398 marks the effective end of Tughlaq central authority.
The Sayyid (1414–1451) and Lodi (1451–1526) dynasties.

These two shorter dynasties ruled over a much-reduced Sultanate, with real power increasingly regional (Bengal, Malwa, Gujarat and the Deccan sultanates had become independent). Sikandar Lodi (r. 1489–1517) is the most notable Lodi ruler, credited with administrative consolidation and the founding of Agra. The dynasty ended when Ibrahim Lodi was defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 — the event that conventionally opens the Mughal period.
Institutions of the Sultanate.
For the examination, it helps to separate four institutional threads that ran through all five dynasties:

items.text: The iqta system:

Revenue-bearing territories (iqtas) were assigned to nobles (iqtadars or muqtis) in return for maintaining a fixed quota of cavalry for the Sultan’s army. This solved the problem of paying a large standing army without a fully monetised, centrally administered treasury, but it also meant that provincial nobles controlled real military and fiscal resources — a persistent source of tension between centre and periphery that recurs, in different institutional forms, throughout the rest of the topic (and, much later, in Mughal jagirdari crisis and in the constitutional centre-province debates of Topics 3 and 6).
Judicial administration:

The Sultan’s court, provincial governors, and appointed judges (qazis) administered justice according to Islamic law (sharia, chiefly through the Hanafi school) for matters involving Muslims, while Hindu subjects generally continued to use their own customary and caste-based dispute-resolution mechanisms (village panchayats, caste councils) for most civil matters — a pattern of legal pluralism, not a single uniform legal code imposed on the whole population.
The military:

Sultanate armies were cavalry-based, funded through the iqta system, and repeatedly tested by the most serious external threat of the period — recurring Mongol invasions from the 1220s through the early fourteenth century. Successful Mongol defence, especially under Balban and Alauddin Khalji, should be treated as a major (and often under-credited) achievement of the Sultanate state.
Society and religion:

The Sultanate ruled over an overwhelmingly non-Muslim population. The jizya (a tax on non-Muslim subjects, exempting them from military service) was levied, though its application varied by ruler and period and was sometimes waived for particular groups. Sufi orders (the Chishti order, associated with figures such as Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti of Ajmer and Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi, is especially important) spread through the countryside during this period, building shrines that became centres of popular devotion attracting both Muslim and Hindu visitors — an important channel of cultural interaction distinct from, and often more locally influential than, state policy itself.

blocks.text: The Mughal Empire (1526–1857): Consolidation and Institution-Building

segments.text: Founding and the Sur interregnum.

Babur, a Central Asian prince descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and then defeated a Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527), establishing Mughal rule in northern India. His son Humayun, however, was driven out of India by the Afghan noble Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and spent roughly fifteen years in exile (including a period at the Safavid Persian court) before reclaiming Delhi in 1555. Sher Shah Suri’s brief interregnum (1540–1545) matters more than its short length suggests: he introduced administrative reforms — a systematic land-revenue survey and assessment, a stable silver currency (the rupiya, ancestor of the modern rupee), an extensive road network including the Grand Trunk Road, and a chain of sarais (rest-houses) supporting trade and communication — that the Mughals, under Akbar in particular, later adopted and refined rather than invented from scratch. This is a useful corrective to any account that treats Mughal administrative achievement as arising purely from Mughal genius; a good part of it was inherited and improved.
Akbar and imperial consolidation (r. 1556–1605).

Akbar is the pivotal figure in Mughal state-building. His reign combined military expansion (bringing Rajputana, Gujarat, Bengal and much of the Deccan frontier under Mughal control, often through a mixture of conquest and alliance — most famously marrying into Rajput royal families and incorporating Rajput nobles into the imperial nobility rather than simply conquering and excluding them) with major administrative reform:

items.text: The
mansabdari system

ranked every noble (mansabdar) with a numerical rank indicating both personal status (zat) and the number of cavalry he was obliged to maintain (sawar). Mansabdars were typically paid through assignment of jagirs (revenue rights over specified territory, conceptually similar to the Sultanate’s iqta but administered as part of a more centralised, rotating system to prevent any noble from building an entrenched regional power base).
The
zabt revenue system

, developed under the finance minister Raja Todar Mal, assessed land revenue based on careful measurement of cultivated land and a ten-year average of crop yields and prices (the dahsala system), aiming for a predictable, sustainable share of agricultural output rather than arbitrary extraction.
Akbar’s
religious policy

is one of the most discussed aspects of his reign. He abolished the jizya on non-Muslim subjects in 1564, promoted a policy summarised by the phrase sulh-i-kul (“peace with all” or universal reconciliation), held interfaith discussions at his court (the Ibadat Khana) with Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Jesuit Christian participants, and proposed a syncretic court-centred devotional practice sometimes called Din-i-Ilahi. Historians debate how far Din-i-Ilahi was a genuine new religion (as older accounts sometimes suggested) versus primarily a symbolic, court-centred loyalty order with limited following beyond Akbar’s immediate circle — but there is broad agreement that Akbar’s overall policy of religious accommodation was both a matter of personal conviction and a deliberate strategy for governing a vast non-Muslim majority population with a comparatively small ruling elite.

segments.text: Jahangir and Shah Jahan (r. 1605–1658 combined).

Jahangir largely continued Akbar’s administrative framework while the empire’s cultural life — miniature painting especially — reached new heights. Shah Jahan’s reign (1628–1658) is remembered chiefly for architectural patronage on an extraordinary scale: the Taj Mahal at Agra (built as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal), the Red Fort and Jama Masjid at Delhi (to which he shifted the capital, renaming it Shahjahanabad), and the Shalimar Gardens at Lahore. These monuments are not merely aesthetic footnotes for the exam; they are physical evidence of the fiscal and administrative capacity Akbar’s reforms had built — building on this scale required a state able to mobilise vast resources reliably over many years.
Aurangzeb and imperial overreach (r. 1658–1707).

Aurangzeb came to power after a war of succession against his brothers (a recurring Mughal pattern, since there was no fixed law of primogeniture — succession was regularly decided by force among rival princes, a structural weakness worth noting explicitly rather than treating each succession war as a one-off crisis). His reign brought the empire to its greatest territorial extent, especially through prolonged campaigns in the Deccan against the Marathas and the Deccan sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda. At the same time, his reign produced the single most historiographically contested religious policy of the whole Mughal period: he reimposed the jizya in 1679, and various contemporary and near-contemporary sources record instances of temple destruction associated with his reign. Older colonial-era and nationalist accounts often portrayed Aurangzeb simply as a religious bigot who reversed Akbar’s tolerant legacy and thereby weakened the empire. More recent scholarship (for example the historian Audrey Truschke’s work, and detailed regional studies by historians such as Richard Eaton) complicates this picture: temple patronage and destruction under Aurangzeb both occurred, but destruction was frequently tied to specific political circumstances — temples associated with rebel rulers or used as symbols of a defeated political rival — rather than a blanket policy against Hindu worship as such, and Aurangzeb also continued to employ large numbers of Hindu nobles (including prominent Rajput commanders) throughout his reign. This remains a genuinely live scholarly debate rather than a settled question, and a strong exam answer should present both the evidence for a harder communal turn under Aurangzeb and the evidence complicating a simple bigot narrative, rather than asserting either position as beyond dispute.

What is much less disputed is the strategic cost of Aurangzeb’s decades-long Deccan wars: they drained the imperial treasury, overextended Mughal military resources across a vast and difficult terrain, and never produced a decisive, lasting victory over Maratha resistance under Shivaji and his successors. This is the strategic overreach historians most consistently point to when explaining why the empire, despite reaching its largest territorial size under Aurangzeb, entered rapid political and fiscal difficulty within a generation of his death.
Administration, economy, and culture under the Mughals.
A few threads deserve separate emphasis because the syllabus explicitly lists them as distinct areas (administration, judiciary, military, economy, education, society, art, architecture, culture):

items.text: Judiciary:

Qazi courts administered Islamic law for Muslims; a chief qazi (qazi-ul-quzat) sat at the imperial centre, with a hierarchy of provincial and local qazis. Non-Muslim communities generally continued to resolve most civil disputes (inheritance, marriage, caste matters) through their own community and caste-based institutions, again illustrating legal pluralism rather than a single uniform legal system.
Economy:

Agriculture remained the overwhelming base of state revenue, but Mughal India also had a large, sophisticated trading economy — textiles (cotton and silk) were a major export, and Indian ports connected to Indian Ocean and, increasingly, European trade networks. European trading companies arrived in stages: the Portuguese first (from 1498, well before the Mughal period began), followed by the Dutch, English (East India Company chartered 1600) and French in the seventeenth century, initially as licensed traders operating under Mughal permission rather than as territorial powers — a status that would change fundamentally after Mughal central authority weakened (the subject of Topic 2).
Culture:

Persian remained the administrative and high-cultural language of the empire, while everyday interaction between Persian, Arabic, Turkic and various South Asian vernaculars contributed to the emergence of Urdu as a literary language. Mughal architecture fused Persian, Central Asian and indigenous Indian building traditions — visible in the evolution from the more austere early Mughal style to the elaborate marble work of Shah Jahan’s monuments. Sufi orders continued to play an important social role, and popular devotional movements (both Sufi and Bhakti) provided channels of religious and cultural exchange that operated somewhat independently of state policy.

blocks.text: Decline of the Mughal Empire: A Multi-Causal Process

segments.text: Mughal decline after Aurangzeb’s death in 1707 was gradual and multi-causal, not a single collapse triggered by one policy or one ruler. A strong answer identifies several interacting causes rather than picking just one:

items.text: Succession disputes:
The absence of a fixed succession law meant every transition of power risked a debilitating war among royal princes, weakening central authority at exactly the moments it most needed strength.
The jagirdari crisis:

Historian Satish Chandra’s influential analysis describes a growing mismatch, by the late seventeenth century, between the number of nobles requiring jagir assignments and the amount of assessed revenue actually available to assign — a structural fiscal problem that predates and helps explain the empire’s post-Aurangzeb difficulties, rather than viewing decline as purely the result of “weak later emperors.”
Regional assertion:

Provincial governors increasingly retained local revenue and authority rather than remitting it to Delhi, effectively becoming autonomous or semi-autonomous rulers while nominally still recognising Mughal sovereignty — Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan and his successors, Awadh under the Nawabs, and Hyderabad under the Nizam are the standard examples.
The Maratha challenge:

Maratha power, built by Shivaji in the mid-seventeenth century and expanded dramatically by his successors and the Peshwa ministers in the eighteenth century, repeatedly raided and eventually dominated large parts of central and northern India, becoming the single most important indigenous military challenge to Mughal authority in the eighteenth century.
Sikh consolidation in Punjab
and recurring
Jat uprisings
near Delhi and Agra further eroded direct Mughal control over core territories.
External invasions:

Nadir Shah’s invasion from Persia and sack of Delhi in 1739 (during which the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond were carried off) inflicted catastrophic material and psychological damage; Ahmad Shah Abdali’s repeated invasions from Afghanistan through the 1750s and 1760s further destabilised the region and culminated in the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), where Abdali decisively defeated the Marathas — a battle that, by weakening the strongest surviving indigenous power, indirectly cleared space for later British expansion.
The rise of the East India Company:

As central authority weakened and regional powers fought each other, the English East India Company exploited this fragmented political landscape to expand from a trading concern into a territorial power — the subject developed fully in Topic 2. The Mughal dynasty survived, nominally, as a symbolic authority (the “shadow emperors” of Delhi) for another century, until the British formally abolished the title after the 1857 uprising.
Iqta:
A Sultanate-era assignment of revenue rights over territory to a noble, in exchange for maintaining a quota of troops.
Mansabdari:
The Mughal ranking system assigning nobles a personal and military rank, determining pay, status and military obligation.
Jagir:
Mughal-era territorial revenue assignment supporting a mansabdar, conceptually descended from the iqta but administered within a more centralised, rotating framework.
Zabt / Dahsala system:
Akbar-era land-revenue assessment based on measured cultivation and a ten-year average of yields and prices.
Jizya:
A tax historically levied on non-Muslim subjects under Islamic-influenced states, in place of military service; its application varied significantly by ruler and period in South Asia.
Sulh-i-kul:
Akbar’s policy phrase, usually translated “peace with all” or “universal reconciliation,” describing his approach to governing a religiously diverse empire.
Qazi:
A judge administering Islamic law, operating within a hierarchy from the imperial centre down to the local level.

blocks.text: Historiographical Debates: How Should This Period Be Read?

segments.text: This eleven-century span is one of the most politically sensitive periods in South Asian historiography, and the exam rewards awareness of why it is contested rather than a single confident verdict.

items.text: The colonial periodisation problem.

The nineteenth-century British historian James Mill’s influential History of British India divided Indian history into “Hindu,” “Muslim” and “British” periods — a framework that treated over a thousand years of enormously varied regional politics as if it were defined mainly by the ruler’s religion. Most professional historians today regard this periodisation as an oversimplification that obscures far more than it explains, since it ignores continuity in administration, economy and society across the supposed dividing lines, and ignores the fact that many “Muslim” states relied heavily on Hindu administrators, generals and allies (and vice versa).
Competing modern narratives.

Partly in reaction to colonial historiography, later nationalist traditions developed their own emphases. Indian nationalist historiography has often stressed syncretism and composite culture (sometimes summarised as Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb, referring to the blending of traditions along the Ganges and Yamuna river basins). Hindu-nationalist historiography has tended to emphasise conquest, temple destruction and cultural rupture. Pakistani textbook historiography has often emphasised continuity between medieval Muslim rule and the later Pakistan Movement, presenting the period as part of a longer history of Muslim political presence in the subcontinent. Professional historians generally regard all three of these frameworks as selective: the historical record contains genuine evidence of cooperation, syncretism, patronage across religious lines, coercion, and destruction, varying enormously by ruler, region and period, and a responsible account resists collapsing eleven centuries into any single verdict.
The Aurangzeb debate specifically

(discussed above) remains the sharpest live disagreement among historians, precisely because it sits at the intersection of religious policy, imperial decline and modern political identity. A strong exam answer notes both the evidence historians cite for a harder religious turn and the evidence cited against reading it as a uniform anti-Hindu policy, and explains why the debate matters rather than declaring it resolved.

segments.text: Preparation Checklist

items.text: Build a dynasty chart first — five Sultanate dynasties, then the Mughal line from Babur to the effective end of central authority — before adding institutional or cultural detail.
Make separate short notes on administration, revenue, military organisation, cultural development and causes of decline, rather than one continuous narrative.
Compare the Sultanate iqta system with the Mughal mansabdari–jagir system directly; the differences (centralisation, rotation, ranking) are a common and high-value exam point.

Keep an evidence bank of 8–10 reliable anchors: Second Battle of Tarain (1192), founding of the Sultanate (1206), Alauddin Khalji’s Mongol defences, Babur’s victory at Panipat (1526), Akbar’s abolition of jizya (1564) and the zabt system, Aurangzeb’s reimposition of jizya (1679), Nadir Shah’s invasion (1739), the Third Battle of Panipat (1761).
Practice one analytical outline answering: “Why did Mughal central authority weaken after 1707, and how much of this was structural versus the result of individual rulers’ choices?”

segments.text: Common Confusions to Avoid

items.text: Do not treat 712–1857 as one continuous empire under one system; five distinct Sultanate dynasties and the separate Mughal dynasty used different institutions across different centuries.

Do not write only political-military chronology. The syllabus explicitly includes administration, economy, judiciary, military, education, society, art and culture, and examiners reward coverage of these dimensions.

Do not explain Mughal decline through one ruler (usually Aurangzeb) or one policy alone; it was a long process combining succession disputes, fiscal structure, regional assertion, indigenous military challenges and external invasion.
Do not present Aurangzeb’s religious policy, or Muslim rule in general, as settled beyond scholarly dispute in either direction; present the debate.

segments.text: Easy Revision Points

items.text: Muhammad bin Qasim’s campaign in Sindh began in 711–712 CE and established an early Muslim political presence in the region, administered initially as a frontier province of the Umayyad Caliphate.
The Delhi Sultanate is conventionally dated from 1206 (following the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192) and included the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties.
Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, beginning Mughal rule in northern India; Sher Shah Suri’s brief interregnum (1540–1545) contributed lasting administrative reforms.

Akbar strengthened imperial administration through the mansabdari system and the zabt/dahsala revenue reforms associated with Raja Todar Mal, and pursued a policy of religious accommodation summarised as sulh-i-kul.
Mughal political power weakened substantially after Aurangzeb’s death in 1707, although the dynasty formally continued as a symbolic authority until 1857.
Architecture, Persianate court culture, regional languages, crafts, trade and religious-cultural interaction are as important to this topic as military conquest.

The subcontinent Muslim rulers entered was already politically fragmented, and Muslim political power itself developed in stages — a frontier province in Sindh, then Central Asian raids, then a settled Sultanate, then a much more centralised Mughal Empire — rather than arriving as one uniform, continuous system.

Institutional capacity (iqta, then mansabdari–jagir, then zabt revenue assessment) explains both how these states could govern a vast, diverse population with a relatively small ruling elite, and why institutional strain — especially the jagirdari fiscal crisis — is central to explaining Mughal decline.

Religious policy varied significantly by ruler and period, from Akbar’s abolition of jizya and pursuit of sulh-i-kul to Aurangzeb’s reimposition of jizya; this variation is itself an important exam point, since it undermines any answer that treats “Muslim rule” as religiously uniform across eleven centuries.

Mughal decline after 1707 resulted from the interaction of succession disputes, fiscal-institutional strain, regional assertion, indigenous military challenge (especially the Marathas) and external invasion (Nadir Shah, Ahmad Shah Abdali) — never from a single cause.

This period is genuinely contested in historiography, and the strongest exam answers acknowledge the debate (particularly around Aurangzeb and around competing nationalist framings of the period) rather than asserting a single settled narrative.
